title: Solids: Surface Area and Volume
tagline: Surface area and volume of cylinder, cone, and sphere, including combined solids and unit conversions.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class X Mathematics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every numerical result in this chapter was independently recomputed. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: This chapter extends plane geometry to three-dimensional solids. Students learn to compute the surface area and volume of the right circular cylinder, right circular cone, and sphere, as well as combinations of these solids (such as a cylinder with a conical top, or a hemisphere surmounted on a cube). The chapter also covers unit conversions (between cm³, m³, litres, and millilitres) and applies these concepts to real-world problems involving capacity, materials, and packaging.

learningOutcomes: State the formulae for the volume and surface area of a cylinder, cone, and sphere (including hemisphere).
Apply the formulae to find unknown radii, heights, or slant heights when two of the three quantities are given.
Solve problems involving combined solids (e.g., a cone on top of a cylinder, a hemisphere inside a cylinder, a sphere with a cylindrical hole).
Convert between volume units: cm³, m³, 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³, 1 litre = 1000 cm³, 1 m³ = 1000 litres.
Solve real-world problems involving capacity, material costs, and packaging.
Verify that formulae are applied correctly by checking dimensions and reasonableness of the answer.

blocks.text: Three-dimensional solids occupy space and have two measures: surface area (the total area of the outer surface) and volume (the amount of space enclosed). The solids studied in ICSE Class X are the cylinder, the cone, and the sphere (including its hemisphere). Each solid has specific formulae that must be applied correctly, paying attention to whether the problem asks for curved surface area, total surface area, or volume. The radius (r) is the distance from the centre to the curved surface; the height (h) is the perpendicular distance between the bases (for cylinder and cone); the slant height (l) is the distance from the vertex to a point on the base edge (for cone); and the diameter is twice the radius.

Labels on a cylinder: r (radius), h (height), 2h (curved height), l (slant height, applicable to cone). Labels on a cone: r (radius), h (vertical height), l (slant height). Labels on a sphere: r (radius). Labels on a hemisphere: r (radius), curved surface vs. total surface.

items: π ≈ 3.14 or 22/7, unless otherwise stated.
For the cone, l = √(r² + h²) (Pythagoras' theorem) when the slant height is not given.
Hemisphere is half a sphere; its total surface area includes the flat circular base (πr²) plus the curved surface (2πr²).
Always identify whether the problem asks for curved surface area or total surface area before applying the formula.

blocks.text: A right circular cylinder has a circular base and a perpendicular height. If the radius of the base is r and the height is h, then: Volume V = πr²h (the area of the base times the height). Curved Surface Area CSA = 2πrh (the area of the side surface, excluding the top and bottom). Total Surface Area TSA = 2πr(r + h) = 2πrh + 2πr² (the curved surface plus the top and bottom circles).

items.text: Find the volume of a cylinder with radius 5 cm and height 10 cm.
Find the total surface area of a cylinder with radius 3 cm and height 7 cm.
A cylindrical water tank has radius 2 m and height 1.5 m. How many litres of water can it hold?
items.note: V = πr²h = π × 2² × 1.5 = 6π m³. Since 1 m³ = 1000 litres, the capacity is 6π × 1000 ≈ 18,840 litres.

items: When finding the volume, always use the perpendicular height, not the slant height.
Curved surface area excludes the top and bottom bases; total surface area includes them.
Unit conversions: 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³, 1 litre = 1000 cm³, 1 m³ = 1000 litres.
π may be taken as 22/7 or 3.14, unless the problem specifies otherwise.

blocks.text: A right circular cone has a circular base and a vertex (apex) directly above the centre of the base. If the radius of the base is r, the vertical height is h, and the slant height is l, then: Volume V = (1/3)πr²h (one-third of the cylinder with the same base and height). Curved Surface Area CSA = πrl. Total Surface Area TSA = πr(r + l) = πr² + πrl (the base circle plus the curved surface). The slant height l is found from r and h using Pythagoras: l = √(r² + h²).

items.text: Find the volume of a cone with radius 6 cm and height 8 cm.
items.note: V = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π × 36 × 8 = 96π. The slant height is found via Pythagoras as a subsidiary step.

items.text: Find the total surface area of a cone with radius 4 cm and slant height 5 cm.
A conical tent has a base radius of 3 m and a height of 4 m. Find the curved surface area of the canvas needed.

items: Always find the slant height l = √(r² + h²) when it is not given.
The volume of a cone is one-third the volume of a cylinder with the same base and height.
Total surface area includes the base; curved surface area excludes it.
When a cone is combined with another solid, identify which faces are exposed and which are hidden.

learn.title: Sphere and Hemisphere: Formulae and Calculations

blocks.text: A sphere is the set of all points in space at a fixed distance (radius r) from a centre point. A hemisphere is half a sphere, cut through the centre. The sphere has no flat faces; the hemisphere has a flat circular base (area πr²) and a curved surface (area 2πr²). Formulae: Sphere volume V = (4/3)πr³, Sphere surface area SA = 4πr². Hemisphere volume V = (2/3)πr³, Hemisphere total surface area TSA = πr² (base) + 2πr² (curved) = 3πr², Hemisphere curved surface area CSA = 2πr².

items.text: Find the surface area of a sphere with radius 7 cm.
Find the volume of a hemisphere with radius 3 cm.
A hemispherical bowl of radius 5 cm is filled with water. How many millilitres of water does it hold? (1 cm³ = 1 mL)
items.note: V = (2/3)πr³ = (2/3)π × 125 = 250π/3 cm³. Since 1 cm³ = 1 mL, the capacity is 250π/3 mL ≈ 261.8 mL.

items: The hemisphere total surface area includes the flat circular base (area πr²) plus the curved surface (area 2πr²).
Curved surface area of a hemisphere is half the sphere's surface area: 2πr².
Unit conversions: 1 cm³ = 1 mL. 1 litre = 1000 cm³.
When a hemisphere is surmounted on a cube or cylinder, the base of the hemisphere coincides with the top face of the other solid, so the exposed area excludes the base.

blocks.text: Many ICSE Class X problems involve combinations of two or more solids, such as a cylinder with a conical top, a hemisphere surmounted on a cube, or a sphere with a cylindrical hole. The key principle is: (1) Compute the surface area or volume of each component separately, then (2) add or subtract as needed, taking care to exclude any faces that are internal (not exposed). For surface area: add the exposed curved surfaces; do NOT add the areas of internal flat faces that are joined together. For volume: add the volumes of the component solids (if the combined solid is the union) or subtract the volume of the removed portion (if the combined solid is the difference).

items.text: A solid consists of a cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 10 cm, with a cone of radius 3 cm and height 4 cm on top. Find the total surface area.
items.note: The total surface area consists of the cylinder's curved surface (60π), the cone's curved surface (15π), and the cylinder's bottom base (9π). The cylinder's top base and the cone's base are joined together and are not exposed.

items.text: A cube of side 6 cm has a hemisphere of radius 3 cm surmounted on its top face. Find the total surface area of the resulting solid.
items.note: The cube has 5 exposed faces (the top face is covered by the hemisphere). The hemisphere contributes its curved surface area only; its flat base is internal and not counted.

items.text: A cylinder of radius 4 cm and height 12 cm has a conical hole of radius 4 cm and slant height 5 cm drilled through it. Find the volume of the remaining solid.
items.note: The volume of the remaining solid is the cylinder volume minus the volume of the conical hole. The cone's vertical height is found via Pythagoras: h = √(l² − r²) = √(25 − 16) = 3 cm.

items: For surface area: add only the exposed curved surfaces; exclude internal flat faces that are joined.
For volume: add the volumes of component solids (union) or subtract the removed portion (difference).
When a cone sits on a cylinder, the top base of the cylinder is not exposed.
When a hemisphere sits on a cube or cylinder, the flat base of the hemisphere is not exposed.
Always identify which faces/areas are internal and should be excluded.

blocks.text: Solid geometry problems often require converting between volume units. The key conversions are: 1 m = 100 cm, 1 m² = 10,000 cm², 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³ (10⁶ cm³), 1 litre = 1000 cm³, and 1 m³ = 1000 litres. When converting, cube the linear conversion factor.

items.text: A cylindrical tank of capacity 2 m³ is filled with water. How many litres of water is this?
A tank holds 250 litres of water. Express this in m³.

items: 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³ (cube the factor 100).
1 litre = 1000 cm³.
1 m³ = 1000 litres.
Always check that the conversion factor is applied correctly (multiply or divide).

blocks.text: The questions that follow move from straightforward formula applications through multi-step problems involving combined solids and unit conversions to reasoning about which faces are exposed. Work each one by identifying the solid(s), writing the relevant formula, and substituting the given values.

questions.prompt: The volume of a cylinder with radius 3 cm and height 7 cm is _____.
questions.explanation: The volume of a cylinder is V = πr²h. With r = 3 cm and h = 7 cm, V = π × 3² × 7 = π × 9 × 7 = 63π cm³.
questions.commonMistake: Misapplying the formula V = πr²h or miscalculating r² × h.

questions.prompt: The total surface area of a sphere of radius 7 cm is _____.
questions.explanation: SA = 4πr² = 4π × 7² = 4π × 49 = 196π cm².

questions.prompt: Find the curved surface area of a cylinder with radius 5 cm and height 12 cm.
questions.explanation: CSA = 2πrh = 2π × 5 × 12 = 120π cm².

questions.prompt: Find the volume of a cone with radius 4 cm and slant height 5 cm.
questions.answer: First find vertical height: h = √(l² − r²) = √(25 − 16) = 3 cm. Then V = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π × 16 × 3 = 16π cm³.
questions.explanation: The vertical height is found via Pythagoras: h = √(l² − r²) = √(25 − 16) = 3. Then V = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π × 16 × 3 = 16π cm³.

questions.prompt: A hemisphere of radius 3 cm is surmounted on a cube of side 6 cm. Find the total surface area of the combined solid.
questions.answer: Total surface area = 6 × 6² – π × 3² + 2π × 3² = 216 – 9π + 18π = 216 + 9π cm² (≈ 244.26 cm² using π = 3.14).
questions.explanation: The cube has 6 faces of area 36 cm² each, so 216 cm². The hemisphere (radius 3 cm) sits on the top face and covers a circle of area π × 3² = 9π cm², which is no longer exposed. The rest of the top face (36 – 9π) stays exposed. The hemisphere adds its curved surface area 2π × 3² = 18π cm². Total = 216 – 9π + 18π = 216 + 9π cm².

questions.prompt: Convert 7500 cm³ to litres.
questions.explanation: Since 1 litre = 1000 cm³, divide by 1000.

questions.prompt: A solid toy is in the form of a hemisphere surmounted on a right circular cone. The height of the cone is 4 cm and the diameter of the base is 6 cm. Determine (i) the volume of the solid toy, (ii) the surface area of the solid toy.
questions.answer: (i) Volume = volume of cone + volume of hemisphere. Cone: r = 3 cm, h = 4 cm, l = √(3² + 4²) = 5 cm. V_cone = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π × 9 × 4 = 12π cm³. Hemisphere: V_hemisphere = (2/3)πr³ = (2/3)π × 27 = 18π cm³. Total V = 12π + 18π = 30π cm³ ≈ 94.2 cm³. (ii) Surface area = CSA of cone + CSA of hemisphere. CSA of cone = πrl = π × 3 × 5 = 15π cm². CSA of hemisphere = 2πr² = 2π × 9 = 18π cm². Total SA = 15π + 18π = 33π cm² ≈ 103.7 cm².
questions.explanation: (i) Cone volume: V = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π × 3² × 4 = (1/3)π × 9 × 4 = 12π. Hemisphere volume: V = (2/3)πr³ = (2/3)π × 3³ = (2/3)π × 27 = 18π. Total = 30π. (ii) Cone curved surface: CSA = πrl where l = √(r² + h²) = √(9 + 16) = 5, so CSA = π × 3 × 5 = 15π. Hemisphere curved surface: 2πr² = 2π × 3² = 18π. The flat base of the hemisphere and the base of the cone are joined and not exposed. Total = 33π.
questions.commonMistake: Including the flat circular base of the hemisphere or the base of the cone in the surface area, which are internal and not exposed.

questions.prompt: The volume of a sphere of radius r is:
questions.explanation: The standard formula for the volume of a sphere is V = (4/3)πr³.

questions.prompt: The curved surface area of a right circular cylinder of radius r and height h is:
questions.explanation: Unrolling the curved surface of a cylinder gives a rectangle of length 2πr and height h, so CSA = 2πrh.

questions.prompt: The slant height l of a cone with radius 3 cm and height 4 cm is:
questions.explanation: For a right circular cone, l = √(r² + h²) = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 cm.

questions.prompt: The total surface area of a hemisphere of radius r is:
questions.explanation: TSA of a hemisphere = curved surface area + base area = 2πr² + πr² = 3πr².

questions.prompt: If a solid sphere is melted and recast into smaller spheres, which quantity remains the same (neglecting wastage)?
questions.explanation: Melting and recasting changes shape but conserves the amount of material, so total volume remains constant.

questions.prompt: The volume of a cone of radius r and height h is:
questions.explanation: A cone has one-third the volume of a cylinder with the same base radius and height: V = (1/3)πr²h.

questions.prompt: The total surface area of a solid hemisphere includes its curved surface and its ______ base.
questions.explanation: A hemisphere has a curved dome and a flat circular face; TSA = 2πr² + πr² = 3πr².

questions.prompt: The volume of a right circular cylinder of radius r and height h is ______.
questions.explanation: Volume of a cylinder equals area of circular base times height, i.e. πr² × h.

questions.prompt: When a solid is melted and recast into another shape, its ______ remains unchanged (without wastage).
questions.explanation: The quantity of material is conserved during melting and recasting, so volume stays the same.

questions.prompt: A solid cylinder of radius 6 cm and height 14 cm is melted and recast into solid spheres of radius 3 cm. Find the number of spheres formed (use π = 22/7).
questions.explanation: Volume of cylinder = πr²h = π × 6² × 14 = 504π cm³. Volume of one sphere = (4/3)πR³ = (4/3)π × 3³ = 36π cm³. Number of spheres = 504π / 36π = 14.

questions.prompt: Find the curved surface area and total surface area of a cone with radius 7 cm and slant height 25 cm (use π = 22/7).
questions.answer: Curved surface area = 550 cm², total surface area = 704 cm².
questions.explanation: CSA = πrl = (22/7) × 7 × 25 = 550 cm². Base area = πr² = (22/7) × 49 = 154 cm². TSA = CSA + base area = 550 + 154 = 704 cm².

questions.prompt: A student calculates the total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius r as 2πr². Analyse the error and give the correct result with reasoning.
questions.answer: The student found only the curved surface area (2πr²) and omitted the flat circular base. A solid hemisphere has both surfaces, so TSA = curved surface area + area of circular base = 2πr² + πr² = 3πr².
questions.explanation: Total surface area must include every exposed surface of the solid; the circular face is part of a solid hemisphere's boundary.

questions.prompt: Two cylinders have equal volumes. Cylinder A has twice the radius of cylinder B. Analyse how their heights compare.
questions.answer: Height of cylinder A is one-fourth the height of cylinder B.
questions.explanation: Volume = πr²h. Let B have radius r and height h_B, A has radius 2r and height h_A. Equal volumes give π(2r)²h_A = πr²h_B, so 4h_A = h_B and h_A = h_B/4. Doubling radius quadruples base area, so height must reduce to one-fourth for same volume.

questions.prompt: When a cone and a cylinder have the same base radius and same height, a student claims their curved surface areas are equal. Analyse this claim.
questions.answer: The claim is generally false. Cylinder CSA = 2πrh, while cone CSA = πrl where l = √(r²+h²) is the slant height. These are equal only in special cases, not in general (for example r=3,h=4 gives cylinder CSA 24π but cone CSA 15π).
questions.explanation: Curved surface area depends on different dimensions: cylinder on height, cone on slant height; equal base and height do not make 2h equal to l.

questions.prompt: A metal sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and recast into a wire of radius 0.2 cm. Analyse the method to find the length of the wire and state the key principle.
questions.answer: Use conservation of volume: volume of sphere = volume of wire (cylinder). (4/3)π(6)³ = π(0.2)²×L, so L = (4/3×216)/(0.04) = 288/0.04 = 7200 cm (72 m). The key principle is that melting and recasting preserves volume (neglecting wastage).
questions.explanation: Equating volumes converts the shape-change problem into an equation for the unknown dimension of the new solid.

keyPoints: Surface area measures the total area of all faces/surfaces of a solid, while volume measures the space occupied by it.
Curved surface area (CSA) excludes base(s), total surface area (TSA) includes all surfaces, and volume uses cubic units.
For a cylinder of radius r and height h: CSA = 2πrh, TSA = 2πr(h+r), Volume = πr²h.
For a cone of radius r, height h and slant height l = √(r²+h²): CSA = πrl, TSA = πr(l+r), Volume = (1/3)πr²h.
For a sphere of radius r: surface area = 4πr², volume = (4/3)πr³; for a hemisphere: CSA = 2πr², TSA = 3πr², volume = (2/3)πr³.
Use consistent units (cm, m) and convert before calculation; area is in square units and volume in cubic units.
When solids are melted and recast, volume is conserved (neglecting wastage unless stated).
For combination solids, add or subtract volumes/surface areas of relevant parts carefully, avoiding double-counting joined faces.
π may be taken as 22/7 or 3.14 as specified; keep symbolic form until the final step when possible.
Identify radius, diameter, height and slant height correctly from the figure or data before substituting in formulas.
examFocus: Write the correct formula first, substitute values with units, and state the final answer with appropriate square/cubic units.
Distinguish clearly between CSA, TSA and volume; read whether a base is open or closed (e.g. bucket, tent, vessel).
For cones, compute slant height using l = √(r²+h²) when not given directly.
In melting/recasting problems, equate volumes and solve for the unknown dimension or number of objects.
In combined solids, identify which surfaces are exposed and which are joined; joined areas are not part of external TSA.
Convert diameter to radius and ensure all dimensions are in the same unit before applying formulas.
Use π = 22/7 when dimensions are multiples of 7 for simpler arithmetic, unless otherwise instructed.
Show intermediate steps (especially volume conservation equations) to secure method marks.

vocabulary.meaning: The area of only the curved surface of a solid, excluding flat bases.
The sum of areas of all surfaces/faces of a solid.
The amount of three-dimensional space occupied by a solid.
The distance from the centre to the boundary of a circular base or sphere.
The distance from the apex of a cone to a point on the edge of its circular base.
Half of a sphere cut by a plane through its centre.
A cylinder whose bases are circles and axis is perpendicular to the bases.
A cone with a circular base and vertex directly above the centre of the base.
Melting a solid and reshaping it into another solid, conserving volume.
The amount a container can hold, often related to its internal volume.
A solid formed by combining two or more basic solids.
The constant ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, approximately 22/7 or 3.14.

figures.caption: Cylinder, cone and sphere with dimensions
figures.description: Three solids are shown side by side: a right circular cylinder labelled with radius r and height h; a right circular cone on a circular base labelled with radius r, vertical height h and slant height l along its surface; and a sphere labelled with radius r. Dashed lines indicate internal heights/radii, and formulas for CSA, TSA and volume are associated with each solid.

figures.caption: Hemisphere and its areas
figures.description: A hemisphere is shown resting on its flat circular face. The curved dome surface is shaded to represent curved surface area 2πr², and the circular base is outlined to represent area πr². Together they indicate total surface area 3πr². Radius r is marked from centre to edge.

figures.caption: Melting and recasting solids
figures.description: A solid metallic sphere on the left is shown with an arrow pointing to several smaller identical spheres on the right, indicating melting and recasting. The diagram is annotated with ‘volume conserved’, showing that the volume of the original sphere equals the total volume of the smaller spheres.
